title: Mixed-Ability Classes

pts: Almost every class has a real spread of levels, even after careful placement testing.
Treating mixed ability as an anomaly to solve, rather than the normal starting condition, leads to planning that's constantly surprised by reality.
Build differentiation into the initial plan, not as a patch applied once a gap becomes obvious.

items: Using the diagnostic grid, note the range for each skill: lowest and highest scores.
Identify learners who are strong in one skill and weak in another (a common pattern).
For the next lesson, note one point where the range will matter most (a reading text, a writing task).
Plan one support and one stretch for that point.
After the lesson, note whether the plan helped.
Map the range for motivation and confidence as well as skill.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A class range for reading (A1 to B1) and a plan:

lines: Learner A: reads fluently; finishes early. → Stretch: an inference question.
Learner B: decodes slowly; understands when read aloud. → Support: text read aloud first; key words glossed.
Most learners: A2. → Main task pitched here.

body: Purpose: to show ability as a spread, not two groups. Content: a horizontal band shaded from light to dark, labelled ‘A1’ at the left and ‘B1’ at the right. Small figures are scattered along it, clustered around the middle but spread to both ends. Three overlapping arcs above show ‘support’, ‘main task’ and ‘stretch’ covering different parts of the band. points.h: Differentiate the Task, Not Just the Learner
pts: Vary the complexity of the task itself, rather than only giving weaker learners a separate, easier worksheet.
A shared task with built-in flexibility keeps the class working together while still meeting learners where they are.
This avoids the social cost of visibly separate 'easy' and 'hard' materials.

v: A reading text; three task cards

items: All learners read the same text (a short story or article).
Offer three task cards at different levels of challenge (see model language).
Learners choose a card or the teacher suggests one; learners can move up a level when they finish.
After the task, pairs from different levels share answers: the story summary helps the true/false group check; the opinion group explains its view.
Keep the discussion shared, so the class works on one text together.
Differentiate the output: some learners write, some draw and label, some record a spoken summary.
Offer the same questions with different amounts of support.
Support: level 1 card.
Stretch: level 3 card.

blocks.x: Three task cards for one story:

lines: Level 1: Put these five pictures in story order. Write one sentence for each.
Level 2: Answer six questions about the story.
Level 3: Was the main character right? Give two reasons from the story.

blocks.x: The same text keeps the class together; the task gives each learner an appropriate challenge.

body: Purpose: to show differentiation by task. Content: one book in the centre. Three doors lead from it, labelled ‘Level 1: order and label’, ‘Level 2: answer questions’, ‘Level 3: give an opinion’. Behind all three doors, the same room: ‘shared discussion’. Style: warm, simple. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free). Three sections for three task levels; learners choose where to start.

blocks.x: Three colours of card for the three task levels.

pts: Tasks with no fixed ceiling — 'write as many sentences as you can' — let each learner perform at their own level naturally.
Stronger learners self-select more ambitious output; weaker learners aren't blocked by a task pitched too high.
Open-endedness removes the need to pre-judge exactly where each learner sits before the task begins.

v: A picture of a busy market scene

items: Show the picture.
Task: ‘Write as many sentences about the picture as you can in eight minutes.’
Every learner starts at their own level: some write There is a cow.; others write A man is trying to sell mangoes to a woman who looks unsure.
Pairs compare and add one sentence from their partner’s list.
Share a range of sentences, celebrating variety.
‘Ask as many questions as you can’ about the picture.
‘Find as many words as you can’ in a word grid.
Support: a word bank beside the picture.
Stretch: sentences must use a structure from this unit.

lines: Write as many sentences as you can.
List all the ways you could use a plastic bottle.
How many questions can you ask the person in this photo?

blocks.x: Why open-ended tasks work in mixed classes: no learner reaches the ceiling, and no learner is blocked at the door.

body: Purpose: to show open-endedness. Content: a staircase that continues upward and off the top of the frame. Learners stand on different steps, all on the same staircase. Caption: ‘Everyone starts; no one finishes.’ Style: friendly, simple. Board version: not applicable.

items: Padlet (free plan). Learners post sentences to a shared wall; count total sentences as a class.

blocks.x: The picture on the board; sentences in notebooks.

body: Count the whole class’s total, not each learner’s. ‘Together we wrote 214 sentences’ motivates every learner, including those who wrote three, and avoids turning an open-ended task into a competition won by the same few learners.

pts: Sentence starters, word banks and models support weaker learners without reducing the cognitive challenge of the task itself.
Scaffolding is temporary by design — it should be removable as competence builds, not a permanent simplification.
The goal is access to the same task, not a different, lesser one.

v: A writing task; three levels of scaffold

items: Lesson 1: learners write a short paragraph (My best friend) using a full frame with gaps.
Lesson 2: a similar task (My favourite teacher) with sentence starters only.
Lesson 3: a similar task (My neighbour) with a word bank only.
Each learner moves at their own pace; some may need the full frame again.
Show learners the three pieces side by side to see their progress.
Apply the same three-step scaffold to speaking (script, prompts, free).
Support: stay at a scaffold level longer.
Stretch: skip to the word bank or free writing.

lines: Full frame: My best friend is ______. She is ______ years old. She likes ______. We ______ together.
Starters: My favourite teacher is… / I like her because… / In her class, we…
Word bank: kind, patient, funny, helps, explains, stories, always

body: Purpose: to show fading support. Content: three images of the same building under construction. In the first, the building is surrounded by full scaffolding. In the second, only some scaffolding remains. In the third, the building stands alone. Beneath each, a label: ‘frame’, ‘starters’, ‘word bank’. Style: clean architectural illustration. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs (free). Three template versions saved in a shared folder.

blocks.x: Three stacks of slips (frame, starters, word bank) at the front; learners take the one they need.

pts: Extension questions and freer production options prevent stronger learners from disengaging through under-challenge.
Stretch tasks should extend the same target language, not simply add unrelated busywork.
Under-challenged strong learners are as much a differentiation failure as unsupported weak ones.

v: Extension cards linked to current tasks

items: For each main task, prepare one extension that deepens it, not just adds more of the same.
Put the extension on a card and let learners take it when they finish.
Make the extension connect back to the class (something they will share).
Vary extensions: creative, analytical, research, teaching others.
Check extensions as seriously as main tasks.
An ‘extension wall’ with cards learners can choose freely.
Stretch: extensions are the stretch.

lines: More (avoid): You finished? Do exercises 5, 6 and 7 too.
Deeper: You finished? Write the story from the dog’s point of view. / Find two sentences in the text where the writer shows, not tells, a feeling. / Prepare a three-question quiz for the class.

body: Purpose: to contrast two kinds of extension. Content: two holes being dug. One is wide and shallow, labelled ‘more of the same’. The other is narrow and deep, reaching water, labelled ‘deeper thinking’. Style: simple, slightly humorous. Board version: not applicable.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers). Stronger learners design visual summaries for the class.

blocks.x: A box of extension cards at the side of the room.

pts: Regroup learners by proficiency, interest or random assignment depending on the specific task's purpose.
Fixed groupings across a whole term calcify into identities ('the weak group') that can undermine motivation.
This connects directly to Unit 7's grouping dynamics, applied specifically to managing ability range.

v: Grouping cards; a record of groupings

items: Plan three different grouping criteria for the week: similar ability (for targeted support), mixed ability (for peer help), and interest or random (for variety).
Match each to a task: similar ability for a focused grammar review; mixed ability for a project; random for a speaking game.
Record groupings so no learner is always in the same group.
At the end of the week, ask learners which groupings helped them.
Let learners choose partners for one task each week.
Support and stretch come from the grouping choice itself.

lines: Similar ability: Today, group A works with me on past forms; group B works on a reading extension.
Mixed ability: Each group has one learner from each colour card.
Random: Pick a number from the tin.
Interest: Cricket fans here; film fans there; music fans by the window.

body: Purpose: to show fluid grouping. Content: three panels showing the same twelve learners in different arrangements: by similar level, mixed, and random. Each learner has a consistent small symbol so the reader can see them move. Style: clear, colourful. Board version: not applicable.

items: Wheel of Names or Classroomscreen group maker (free). Random groups in seconds.

blocks.x: Numbered lollipop sticks in a tin.

pts: Deliberately pairing stronger and weaker learners can benefit both, but only if roles are structured rather than left informal.
Give the stronger learner a specific supporting role (checker, model) rather than an open-ended 'help them' instruction.
Unstructured pairing risks the stronger learner simply doing the task for the weaker one.

items: Pair a more confident learner with a less confident one.
Give clear roles: the ‘coach’ checks and prompts; the ‘player’ does the task.
Give the coach a checklist of what to look for and prompt questions (not answers).
Swap roles on a different task where the other learner is stronger, if possible.
Ask both learners what they learned.
‘Expert groups’: learners who master a point first teach it to others.
Reciprocal reading: pairs take turns summarizing and questioning.
Support: the player gets the coach’s help.
Stretch: the coach deepens their own understanding by explaining.

lines: Check the verb. Is it past?
Read the sentence again. Does it sound right?
What word could you use instead?

blocks.x: What the coach should not do: take the pen and write the answer. Peer tutoring research suggests benefits for both tutors and tutees when roles are structured (Topping 2005).

body: Purpose: to show structured roles. Content: two learners at a desk. One writes (‘player’); the other holds a small checklist card and points, with a speech bubble containing a question, not an answer. Style: friendly, inclusive. Board version: not applicable.

items: Printable role cards made in Canva for Education (free for teachers).

blocks.x: Handwritten role cards, laminated for reuse.

body: Explaining something to someone else is one of the most effective ways to learn it. Research on peer tutoring often finds that tutors gain as much as, or more than, the learners they help, provided the tutoring is structured (Topping 2005).

pts: Avoid rigid 'high/low' groupings that harden into fixed identities learners internalise.
Rotate grouping criteria regularly so no learner is permanently cast in one ability role.
Ability is task-dependent and developing, not a fixed trait — grouping practice should reflect that.

v: Class list; a record of roles and groups

items: Check your language: replace ‘the weak group’ and ‘the bright ones’ with task-based descriptions (‘the group working on past forms’).
Keep a record of which learners take which roles (leader, reporter, coach, player).
Rotate roles weekly so every learner leads sometimes.
Notice learners who surprise you, and record it.
Tell learners regularly that ability grows with practice, and point to evidence in their own work.
Ask learners to record one thing they did well this week that they could not do last month.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Instead of the weak group, say the group working on reading aloud today.
Instead of You’re good at English, say You practised a lot, and it shows in your writing.

blocks.x: Growth language (Dweck 2006): You can’t do this yet. / This is hard, which means you’re learning.

Purpose: to show fixed versus flexible labels. Content: two learners. One wears a heavy, permanent badge reading ‘weak’. The other holds a small, changeable card reading ‘working on: past forms’. Style: gentle, non-judgemental. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets (free). A roles log with a column per week.

body: For two weeks, give every learner a leading role at least once: reporter, group chair, coach or presenter. Record who surprised you. Most teachers find at least one learner whose ability they had underestimated.

dek: Unit 15 of 100: differentiation isn't a special accommodation for a few learners — it's the default design condition of almost every real class.

aims.x: This unit treats a wide range of ability as the normal condition of a class rather than a problem to be solved. It offers practical ways to design tasks, support and grouping so that every learner is working at an appropriate level of challenge.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: plan for a range of ability from the start;
differentiate tasks rather than simply separating learners;
design open-ended tasks with no fixed ceiling;
scaffold for weaker learners without lowering the challenge;
stretch stronger learners with purposeful extension;
group flexibly according to the purpose of each task;
structure peer teaching so that both partners benefit;
avoid labels that harden into fixed identities.

why: Why this matters. A scheme of work (Unit 14) still has to land in a room with a real spread of ability. Differentiation is where the plan meets that spread.

background.x: Every class is mixed. Even learners placed by the same test differ in reading speed, confidence, vocabulary, home-language literacy, motivation, prior schooling and a dozen other ways. In many Indian classrooms the range is especially wide: a single Grade 8 class may include learners who read English fluently and learners still decoding simple words, learners who hear English at home and learners who hear it only at school. Natalie Hess (2001) calls these ‘large multilevel classes’ and argues that they are not an exception to good teaching but its everyday setting.

Differentiation is the name for planning with this range in mind. Carol Ann Tomlinson (2014) describes it as adapting content, process or product so that each learner can work at a level of challenge that promotes growth. It does not mean writing thirty lesson plans. Most differentiation comes from a few well-chosen designs: tasks with several entry points, support that can be removed as learners grow, extensions that deepen rather than lengthen, and grouping that changes with purpose.

The theoretical basis for much of this lies in Lev Vygotsky’s idea of the zone of proximal development: the space between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help (Vygotsky 1978). David Wood, Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross (1976) described the help that moves learners across this zone as scaffolding, temporary support that is gradually withdrawn. Unit 83 returns to this theory in depth.

A warning belongs here too. Labels such as ‘weak’ and ‘bright’ tend to become self-fulfilling. Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson’s classic study (1968), though debated in its details, drew attention to how teachers’ expectations can shape learners’ progress. Good differentiation avoids fixing learners in place.

items: Tiered task outcomes. Assess each learner against the task level they chose, and track movement between levels over a term.
Open-ended output. Compare individual output on an open-ended task at the start and end of a term.
Scaffold independence. Record the scaffold level each learner needs for writing; aim for movement towards independence.
Role rotation. Check that every learner has taken each role at least once in a term.
How wide is the range in your class? How do you know?
When learners finish early, what do they do? Is it deeper or just more?
How do you describe learners, aloud and in your head? How might those words shape their progress?
Which grouping pattern do you use most? Why?
Who in your class has surprised you recently? What did you learn from it?

terms.def: Adapting teaching, tasks, support or outcomes so that learners of different levels and needs in the same class can all make progress.
An additional, more challenging task for learners who finish early or need stretch, designed to deepen the same learning rather than simply add more of the same work.
Grouping learners in different ways for different purposes, by level, interest or mixed ability, and changing groups regularly so that no learner is fixed in one ‘level’.
The belief that ability can grow through effort, good strategies and help, as opposed to a fixed mindset, which sees ability as unchangeable (Dweck 2006).

A class in which learners differ in proficiency, aptitude, pace, interests and learning needs; in practice every class is mixed-ability, and teaching responds through differentiation, tiered and open-ended tasks, and flexible grouping.
A class, often large, in which learners are at clearly different levels of proficiency; Natalie Hess (2001) argues that such classes are the everyday setting of teaching, not an exception to it.
A task with more than one acceptable answer or outcome, which learners at different levels can complete to different depths, making it useful in mixed-ability classes.
Arranging for learners to teach one another, for example explaining a point to a partner, structured so that both partners benefit.
A structured arrangement in which one learner tutors another; research suggests that tutors often gain as much as tutees when roles are well organized (Topping 2005).

Temporary support that helps learners do what they could not yet do alone, gradually withdrawn as competence grows (Wood, Bruner and Ross 1976). Examples include sentence frames, modelling, visual prompts and guiding questions.

The tendency for a teacher’s expectations of learners to influence their performance, through differences in attention, questioning and feedback (Rosenthal and Jacobson 1968). Low expectations of ‘weak’ learners can become self-fulfilling.
A task prepared at several levels of challenge on the same content, so that learners of different abilities can all work on the same topic, for example three versions of a reading task.

The gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with support from a teacher or more capable peer (Vygotsky 1978). Teaching aimed within this zone, with scaffolding, promotes development.
